The paper presents a method for exploring feasible design spaces that satisfy heterogeneous constraints.
The approach involves classifying constraints and solvers, pruning design spaces, and composing forward and inverse problem solvers.
The method is demonstrated on several real-world design problems, including designing a car hood latch and a machine part.
The authors classify IP-solvers based on the properties of design constraints, such as locality and continuity.
The authors use a Pareto-tracing levelset topology optimization method to incorporate manufacturability constraints into the design process.
The overlap measure is used to filter the augmented TSF and incorporate accessibility constraints into the design process.
The proposed approach may sacrifice optimality when applying corrections to the geometry or topology of a solution to make it manufacturable.
The classification of solvers based on the types of constraints they can handle is essential for organizing them into workflows that satisfy heterogeneous constraints.
The TSF is used to steer the optimization process and measure the global changes in violation of constraints with respect to local topological punctures.
The maximal elements are implicitly defined by pointwise constraints and are used to prune design spaces without premature optimization.
Unsweep generates a design that remains within a given region of space while moving according to a prescribed motion.
PareTO generates a design that satisfies the compliance target with minimal mass.
